what-is-git-and-github-install-and-setup: Git = a program on your computer that keeps the history of a project in a hidden `.git` folder. Works offline.
GitHub = a website that stores Git projects online: backup, sharing, teamwork, a place to show your work.
GitLab and Bitbucket do the same job as GitHub. The Git commands stay the same.
Tell Git who you are once: `git config --global user.name` and `user.email`
`--global` = use this setting for every project on this computer.
your-first-git-repository-init-add-commi: Three places: working folder, staging area, repository (history).
`git init` makes the folder a repository. `git status` shows what is going on and is always safe.
`git add` moves changes to staging. `git commit -m "message"` saves them as a snapshot.
`git log --oneline` shows the history, newest first. `git diff` shows what you changed.
`.gitignore` lists files Git should skip (`*.log`, `node_modules/`, `.env`). It only works on files not yet tracked.
Commit small and often. One commit = one change you can explain in a short sentence.
undo-mistakes-restore-amend-revert: Unsaved edit you want gone: `git restore file`. Careful, it cannot be brought back.
Fix the last commit: `git commit --amend`. Only if you have not pushed it.
Undo a shared commit safely: `git revert`. It adds a new commit that does the opposite.
Dangerous: `git reset --hard`, `git push --force`, `git clean -fd`. Know what they delete before you run them.
Lost a commit? `git reflog` is the safety net.
git-branches-and-merging: A branch is a movable label that points to a commit. Try ideas on a branch, keep `main` stable.
`git switch -c name` creates a branch and moves to it. `git switch main` goes back.
Switch to the branch that should receive the work, then `git merge other-branch`.
Fast-forward merge: `main` had not moved, so Git just moves the label. No merge commit.
`git branch -d name` deletes a merged branch. Git refuses if it is not merged.
Commit or stash your work before you switch branches.
resolve-git-merge-conflicts: A conflict = both branches changed the same lines. It is not an error. Git asks you to decide.
`git status -s` shows `UU` for the file with the conflict.
Open the file, choose the final text, and delete all three marker lines: `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`.
Never commit a file that still has markers. Search the project for `<<<<<<<`.
Lost in the middle of it? `git merge --abort` takes you back.
github-remotes-push-pull-and-clone: A remote is another copy of your repository, usually on GitHub. The default name is `origin`.
First push: `git push -u origin main`. `git remote -v` lists your remotes.
`git clone url` copies a whole repository with its history and sets `origin` for you.
`git fetch` downloads changes without touching your files. `git pull` fetches and merges.
Sign in with Git Credential Manager, a personal access token or an SSH key. Never put tokens in a project file or a chat.
Daily rhythm: pull, work, commit, push.
pull-requests-forks-and-code-review: Pull request flow: branch, commit, push, open the pull request, review, merge.
Good PR: short title, a description of what and why, small size, link the issue (`Closes #12`).
Read your own diff on the PR page before you ask anyone to review it.
Fork = your own copy of someone else's project. Contribute from a branch on your fork, then open a PR.
Keep a fork up to date from the original repository before you start new work.
A red check: read the log, fix, push again. Be patient and thank your reviewers.
good-commits-gitignore-and-keeping-secre: A good commit message says what changed and why, in a short line.
Small, focused commits make history easy to read and easy to undo.
Never commit: secrets, personal data, `node_modules/`, build folders, large binaries, `.DS_Store`.
Keep secrets in a `.env` file and list `.env` in `.gitignore`.
Committed a secret? Treat it as stolen: revoke it and create a new one first. Cleaning the history comes second.
A README is the front door of the project. Add a licence if others may reuse it.
stash-tags-and-exploring-history: `git stash` puts unfinished work aside. `git stash pop` brings it back. `git stash drop` deletes it.
A tag names an important moment, such as a release.
`git log --oneline --graph --all` shows branches. `git log -5` shows the last five commits.
`git show HEAD` shows the latest commit. `git diff main feature` compares two branches.
`git blame file` shows who changed each line and when. Use it to find the commit that explains a line.
`git cherry-pick` takes one commit. Use `rebase` with care, never on shared history.
git-and-github-for-your-job-search-and-c: Profile: professional username and photo, a one-line bio, links to LinkedIn or your resume.
A repository named exactly like your username shows its README on your profile.
Pin your best projects. A README needs: a one-line description, screenshot, features, tech, install steps that work, what you learned.
Never publish secrets, personal data or an employer's confidential code.
Use the GitHub no-reply email if you do not want your real email in commits.
Be honest: show what you really built, and say what you learned or what is next.

what-is-python-install-and-first-program: Windows: tick **Add python.exe to PATH** on the first installer screen. Missing it is the most common setup problem.
Check the install: `python --version` should start with 3.
The interactive prompt is for trying one line. A file (`hello.py`) is for a real program.
Read error messages from the bottom up: the last line says what went wrong, and the line number says where.
Curly quotes copied from a web page break code. Retype them as straight quotes.
variables-numbers-strings-and-input: A variable is a name that points to a value: `price = 120`.
`input()` always gives text. Convert it: `int(...)` or `float(...)`.
Not sure what a value is? `print(value, type(value))`.
For money, round on purpose with `round(x, 2)` and remember that floats are not always exact.
Common mistakes: adding text to a number, and using a name before you create it.
making-decisions-with-if-elif-else: `if` / `elif` / `else`: the first true branch runs and the rest are skipped. `else` has no condition.
Every `if`, `elif` and `else` line ends with a colon, and the code under it is indented.
Test each branch with values on both sides of the boundary.
lists-and-loops-for-while: A list is ordered and can change: `prices = [120, 80]`. Counting starts at 0.
`append` adds at the end, `remove` takes out a value, `sorted(list)` gives a new sorted list.
A slice `prices[1:3]` stops before the second number.
`for item in items:` runs once for each item. `range(3)` is 0, 1, 2: it stops before the number.
`break` leaves the loop. `continue` skips to the next round.
Do not change a list while you loop over it. Copy it first with `list(x)` or `x[:]`.
dictionaries-tuples-and-sets: Dictionary = look up by key: `product["stock"]`. A missing key raises `KeyError`.
`product.get("colour", "none")` gives a default instead of an error.
`.items()` loops over key and value together. `"price" in product` checks a key.
Tuple = small fixed group (coordinates). Set = unique values and fast `in` checks.
List for order, dictionary for lookup, tuple for fixed, set for unique.
functions-in-python: `def name(parameters):` defines a function. It only runs when you call it.
`return` sends a value back. No `return` means the call gives `None`.
A default value makes a parameter optional: `rate=0.18`. You can pass it by name.
A function can return two values. Python packs them into a tuple: `low, high = min_max(x)`.
Variables made inside a function live only there (scope).
One job per function, a verb in the name, return values instead of only printing.
Never use an empty list as a default value. It is shared between calls.
working-with-text-strings-in-python: Text is a sequence: `text[0]` is the first character, `text[-1]` the last.
`strip()` trims spaces. `lower()`, `upper()` and `replace()` give a new text. The old one does not change.
`split(",")` makes a list. `" ".join(words)` glues a list back together.
Lower the text first before you compare: `name.lower().endswith(".pdf")`.
f-strings format output: `f"{price:.2f}"`, `<10` left-aligns and `>8` right-aligns.
Do not memorise every method. Know they exist and look them up.
read-and-write-files-csv-and-json: Use `with open(...) as f:` so the file is closed for you.
`for line in f:` reads one line at a time, good for big files.
CSV: `csv.DictReader` and `csv.DictWriter` work with rows as dictionaries.
JSON: `json.dumps` turns data into text, `json.loads` turns it back. Use `indent=2` to read it.
`pathlib.Path` builds paths that work on every system.
`FileNotFoundError`? Print `Path("file").resolve()` and see where Python is looking.
handling-errors-with-try-except: An exception is Python's way to stop and say what went wrong. `try` / `except` lets you handle it.
Catch specific errors (`ValueError`), not a bare `except:` that hides every problem.
Keep the `try` block small so you know which line failed.
`else` runs if nothing failed. `finally` always runs.
Tell the user what went wrong and what to do next.
Use `raise` for your own errors. A custom exception gives a problem a clear name.
Read a traceback from the bottom up.
modules-pip-and-virtual-environments: `import math` or `from math import ceil`. The standard library is already installed.
Your own file `tools.py` can be imported as a module.
`if __name__ == "__main__":` runs code only when the file is run directly, not imported.
`pip install package` adds a package from the internet.
Make a virtual environment per project: `python -m venv .venv`, then activate it.
`pip freeze > requirements.txt` saves the list. `pip install -r requirements.txt` rebuilds it.
Do not name your file like a module (`random.py`). It hides the real one.
classes-and-objects-in-python: A class is a blueprint. An object is one thing made from it: `Wallet("Asha", 500)`.
`__init__` runs when the object is made. `self` is the object itself.
A dataclass is a short way to write a class that only holds data.
Inheritance: `class Savings(Wallet)` reuses and extends another class.
Classes are optional. Use one when data and its actions belong together.
useful-python-standard-library: Dates: `datetime` and `timedelta`. Store dates in ISO format (`2026-10-31`).
`Counter` counts items. `defaultdict` starts new keys with a default value.
`zip(a, b)` pairs two lists. `sorted(items, key=..., reverse=True)` sorts by your rule.
`any(...)` is true if one item matches. `all(...)` is true if every item matches.
Use `help(module)` to learn a module fast.
analyse-a-csv-file-with-python: Plan first: what is in the file and what question do you want answered?
`Path(__file__).parent` finds files next to the script, wherever you run it from.
Read rows with `csv.DictReader`, convert amounts to numbers, and total them by category.
`defaultdict(float)` makes the first total start at `0.0`.
`sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)` puts the biggest first.
Check your result by adding up a few rows by hand.
automate-files-and-folders-with-python: Practise on copies, never on your only copy of a file.
Dry run first: print what you would do, change nothing, then run it for real.
Never overwrite silently. Check if the target exists. Moving is safer than deleting.
`iterdir()` lists a folder, `rglob("*.pdf")` searches all sub-folders.
`item.suffix.lower()` gives the file ending. `mkdir(exist_ok=True)` makes a folder safely.
`shutil.move` moves a file. `shutil.copytree` copies a folder.
final-project-expense-tracker-and-next-s: Plan before you code: data, commands, functions, rules, safety.
Store expenses as a list of dictionaries in a JSON file. A missing file means an empty list.
`argparse` builds the commands (`add`, `list`, `total`) and the `--help` text for you.
`type=float` makes argparse check the amount for you.
Test with `unittest` and a separate `--file`, so your real data is safe.
Next: practise a little every day, then build projects you care about.

what-is-sql-and-a-database: A database stores data in tables. A table has columns (the kind of fact) and rows (one record each).
Primary key = "who am I?" Foreign key = "who do I belong to?"
One language, many engines: SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle. The basics are the same.
Used by analysts, developers, testers, support and finance teams.
Practise in this course on a small shop database.
set-up-sqlite-practice-database: Easiest start: DB Browser for SQLite, the `sqlite3` command line, or an online SQLite playground.
The shop database has 4 tables: `customers` (8 rows), `products` (8), `orders` (10), `order_items` (15).
Check it worked: `SELECT * FROM customers;` returns 8 rows, and Hari Singh has no city.
Every statement ends with a semicolon. Keywords are not case sensitive, but write them in capitals to read easily.
Type the queries yourself. Typing makes the shape stick.
Something broke? Delete the file and run the setup script again.
select-from-where-basics: `SELECT columns FROM table;` chooses what to show. `SELECT *` means every column.
`AS` gives a column a nicer name: `price AS cost`.
`WHERE` keeps only the rows that match: `WHERE city = 'Pune'`. Text goes in single quotes.
Missing values: use `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`. Never `= NULL`.
The database thinks in this order: `FROM`, then `WHERE`, then `SELECT`.
Common mistakes: missing quotes around text, and double quotes instead of single.
filter-with-and-or-in-between-like: `AND`: both conditions must be true. `OR`: at least one must be true.
Mixing `AND` and `OR`? Use brackets so the meaning is clear.
`IN ('A', 'B')` is a short way to write many `OR`s.
`LIKE` matches patterns: `%` is any text, `_` is one character. `LIKE 'A%'` starts with A.
Build the filter in small steps and run it each time.
order-by-limit-distinct: `ORDER BY price DESC` sorts the biggest first. The default is `ASC`. Add a second column to break ties.
`LIMIT 3` gives the first three rows. SQL Server uses `TOP 3`.
`CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` is if / then inside a query.
aggregate-functions-count-sum-avg: `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` summarise many rows into one value. `ROUND(AVG(x), 2)` makes it tidy.
If no rows match: `COUNT` gives 0, but `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` give `NULL`.
You can calculate inside an aggregate: `SUM(price * quantity)`.
`MIN` and `MAX` also work on text and dates.
Common mistake: mixing a normal column with an aggregate and no `GROUP BY`.
group-by-and-having: `GROUP BY city` makes one result row for each city.
Every plain column in `SELECT` must be in `GROUP BY`.
`NULL`s are grouped together as one group.
`WHERE` filters rows before grouping. `HAVING` filters groups after. Aggregates go in `HAVING`.
Order of a query: `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `SELECT`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`.
primary-foreign-keys-table-design: One big table causes copies, mistakes and lost facts. Split by kind of thing.
Primary key: every row has its own unique id that never repeats.
Foreign key: a column that points to the primary key of another table (`orders.customer_id`).
One-to-many: one customer, many orders. Many-to-many needs a link table (`order_items`).
To read a new database: find the tables, the keys, and how they link.
Good names help: singular or plural, but be consistent, and `customer_id` for links.
sql-joins-inner-left: A join puts related rows from two tables side by side with `ON a.id = b.customer_id`.
`INNER JOIN` keeps only rows that match on both sides.
`LEFT JOIN` keeps every row from the left table, with `NULL` where there is no match.
Rows with no match: `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.id IS NULL`.
Give tables short aliases (`orders AS o`) and join three tables one at a time.
Results grow when one row matches many. Check the row count after a join.
`FULL OUTER JOIN` is missing in MySQL. `CROSS JOIN` pairs every row, usually a bug.
subqueries-exists-and-ctes: A subquery is a query inside brackets. It can return one value, or a list for `IN`.
`NOT IN` with a `NULL` in the list returns nothing. Use `NOT EXISTS` instead.
`EXISTS` asks: is there at least one matching row?
A subquery in `FROM` works like a temporary table.
`WITH name AS (...)` is a CTE: it names a step so the query reads top to bottom.
Pick the one you can explain in one sentence. Readability matters.
insert-update-delete-safely: `INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...)` adds a row.
`UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE ...` changes rows.
`UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `WHERE` changes every row. Type the `WHERE` first.
Safety: `SELECT` first with the same `WHERE`, check the row count, use a transaction.
`BEGIN`, then `COMMIT` to keep or `ROLLBACK` to undo.
create-table-data-types-constraints: `CREATE TABLE name (column type constraints, ...)` makes a table.
Types: `INTEGER` for ids and counts, `DECIMAL(10,2)` for money, `TEXT` or `VARCHAR`, `DATE`.
`FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES` stops links to rows that do not exist.
`ALTER TABLE` changes a table later. `DROP TABLE` removes it completely. Be careful.
Store only the personal data you really need.
window-functions-row-number-rank: A window function calculates across related rows but keeps every detail row: `function() OVER (...)`.
`ROW_NUMBER()` numbers rows. Add `PARTITION BY` to restart for each group.
Latest row per customer: number rows by date descending, keep number 1.
`RANK` leaves gaps after ties. `DENSE_RANK` does not.
`SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY date)` gives a running total.
`LAG` and `LEAD` look at the previous or next row.
`GROUP BY` gives one row per group. A window keeps all rows.
indexes-and-query-performance: An index is like a book's index. The database finds rows without reading the whole table.
`EXPLAIN` shows the plan. Look for a full table scan on a big table.
Index columns used in `WHERE`, in joins (foreign keys) and in `ORDER BY` on big tables.
Indexes cost space and slow down writes, so do not index everything.
An index is not used with a function on the column, `LIKE '%text'`, or a type mismatch.
Name the columns instead of `SELECT *`, and add `LIMIT` when you need only a few rows.
sql-interview-questions-and-next-steps: Repeat the question in your own words and ask about unclear parts: ties, `NULL`s, what counts as active.
Say your plan before typing. Start simple, run it, then add conditions.
Check your result by counting a few rows by hand.
Mention edge cases: `NULL`s, ties, customers with no orders.
If you do not know, say so and explain how you would find out.
Next: practise weekly, try PostgreSQL or MySQL, learn dates and views, connect SQL to Python or Node.js, and build a small project on GitHub.

what-is-nodejs-and-your-first-script: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser: servers and APIs, command line tools, build tools, scheduled jobs.
Check the install: `node -v` should show `v20` or higher. After installing, open a new terminal.
The REPL (`node`) is for trying one line. A file (`node app.js`) is for a real script.
Different from the browser: no `document` and no `window`, but you get files and the system.
This course builds a tasks API with Express.
modules-npm-and-package-json: Turn on ES modules with `"type": "module"` in `package.json`. Then use `import` and `export`.
Built-in modules are imported with the `node:` prefix: `import os from 'node:os'`.
`npm install express` adds a package. It goes in `dependencies` in `package.json`.
`^5.1.0` in `package.json`: the caret allows newer minor and patch versions, not a new major one. `npm run name` runs a script.
Check a package before you install it: name, downloads, last update.
files-paths-and-built-in-modules: Build paths with `path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'tasks.json')`. It works on every system.
`ENOENT` means the file does not exist. Catch it and return a safe default, such as `[]`.
`mkdir(folder, { recursive: true })` is safe to run twice.
`rm` has no recycle bin. A file store is fine for learning, not for many users.
Never save secrets as plain text in a committed file.
async-javascript-promises-and-event-loop: Node has one thread and an event loop. Slow work (files, network) runs in the background.
A Promise is a value that arrives later. `await` waits for it inside an `async` function.
Independent jobs: `await Promise.all([a(), b()])` is faster than one after the other.
Forgot `await`? You get a Promise, not the value.
Do not block the event loop with long loops or `*Sync` functions inside a server.
your-first-http-server-with-node: Request in, response out. Methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes.
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 bad request, 401 log in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 429 slow down, 500 server broke.
A plain Node server works but gets long. Express makes routing short.
`EADDRINUSE` means another program, or an old copy of your server, is using the port.
Do not leave a test server open to the world.
your-first-express-server: `app.get(path, handler)` runs the handler for a GET on that path. `app.listen(port)` starts the server.
`res.json(object)` is the main way to answer an API call. `res.status(404).json({ error: '...' })` chains.
`res.status(204).end()` is an empty answer, used after a delete.
Send one response per request. A second `res.send` causes an error.
`node --watch` restarts on every save. Use `process.env.PORT` for the port.
`Cannot GET /x` = no route for that path and method.
express-routing-params-query-and-routers: Query string: `/api/tasks?done=true` gives `req.query.done`. Quote the URL in curl.
Status codes: 200 read or update, 201 created, 204 deleted, 400 bad data, 404 missing.
Use `express.Router()` to split routes into files and mount them with `app.use('/api/tasks', router)`.
Keep URLs predictable: plural nouns, no verbs.
express-middleware-explained: Middleware is a function `(req, res, next)`. It either answers, or calls `next()`.
Order is everything: middleware runs in the order you write `app.use`.
`express.json()` reads a JSON body into `req.body`. Bad JSON gives a 400 error.
Use middleware for some routes only: `app.get('/x', check, handler)`.
Request hangs? A middleware forgot to answer or to call `next()`.
build-a-rest-api-crud-routes: Test every route with curl, including the failing cases.
PUT replaces the whole thing. PATCH changes some fields.
Return the new or updated object so the front end does not need a second call.
Early version problems: no validation, data lost on restart, ids not safe.
validation-and-error-handling-in-express: Never trust the request. Check every field on the server.
Write a validation function and return `400` with a clear message when the data is wrong.
Add a `404` handler after all routes for unknown URLs.
One central error handler `(err, req, res, next)` gives every error the same JSON shape.
Front-end validation is for convenience. Server validation is for security.
Do not leak details such as stack traces to the client.
environment-variables-and-saving-data-to: Settings and secrets do not belong in code. Read them from `process.env`.
Put them in a `.env` file and list `.env` in `.gitignore`.
Commit a `.env.example` with names but no real values.
Fail early at startup if a required variable is missing.
A leaked secret stays in git history. Change the secret, do not only delete the line.
A file store is fine to learn. For real apps use a database.
mongodb-and-mongoose-for-your-api: MongoDB stores documents. Mongoose adds schemas and models.
A schema sets the rules: `required`, `trim`, `maxlength`, `default`, `timestamps: true`.
A bad id like `/api/tasks/abc` should give a 404 or 400, not a 500.
Never put the database address in code. Do not open the database to the whole internet.
user-login-with-password-hashing-and-jwt: Never store a password. Store a hash made with `bcrypt`. `bcrypt.compare` is slow on purpose.
After login, the server gives a signed token (JWT). The client sends it on each request.
A middleware checks the token and sets `req.user` before protected routes.
Each user sees only their own tasks: filter by the user id.
Give the same error for a wrong email and a wrong password.
Not covered: logout, refresh tokens, password reset, roles. Use tested libraries for these.
secure-your-express-api-cors-helmet-rate: CORS: allow only your own front end origin.
Rate limiting stops too many requests, especially on login routes.
Keep secrets out of git and logs. Run `npm audit` and keep packages updated.
Use HTTPS in production, check ownership of every record, and take backups.
These steps reduce risk. They do not make an app unhackable.
test-and-deploy-your-node-api: Make the app testable: export `app` and call `listen` in a separate file.
Tests with the built-in `node:test`. `npm test` should pass before every deploy.
For production set `NODE_ENV=production`, use real secrets and a real database.
Keep it running with `pm2`. Put nginx in front with HTTPS.
Add a `/api/health` route and check the logs.
Deploy routine: pull, install, test, restart. Test your backup, and have a way to go back.

excel-screen-cells-first-sheet: A file is a workbook. Inside are worksheets. Each cell has an address: column letter plus row number (`C4`).
A range uses a colon: `A1:C5` is the block from A1 to C5.
The formula bar shows what is really in the cell. The Name Box shows the address.
`Ctrl+Arrow` jumps to the end of the data. `Ctrl+Z` undoes. Do not be afraid to try.
One table, one purpose: headings in row 1, no empty rows or columns inside.
Type `120`, not `Rs. 120` or `120 rupees`. Keep numbers as pure numbers.
enter-and-format-data: Numbers align right, text aligns left. A date is a number that is shown as a date.
A number that looks right but will not add up may be stored as text. Check the alignment.
Formats change only the look: Currency, Percentage (`18%` is stored as 0.18), Date, Text.
Freeze the heading row: View, Freeze Panes, Freeze Top Row.
Avoid merged cells inside data, blank rows or columns in a table, and too many colours.
The AutoFill handle (small square on the corner) copies and continues patterns.
first-formulas-and-cell-references: Every formula starts with `=`. Without it, Excel shows the text.
Click cells while you type instead of typing addresses.
Copy a formula down and the references move with it (relative).
`$` locks a reference: `$J$1` stays fixed when you copy the formula down. Use it for a single input, such as a tax rate.
Do not type numbers inside formulas. Refer to the cell, so a changed price changes the answer.
Errors: `#VALUE!` is text mixed with numbers, `#REF!` is a deleted cell.
sum-average-count-min-max: Functions look like `=SUM(D2:D11)`: name, brackets, range.
`SUM`, `AVERAGE`, `MIN`, `MAX`. `COUNT` counts numbers, `COUNTA` counts non-empty cells, `COUNTBLANK` counts empty ones.
Select cells and look at the status bar for a quick sum and average.
`ROUND(x, 2)` rounds the value. Formatting only changes how it looks.
Percent of total: `=D2/SUM($D$2:$D$11)` with the total locked.
`#DIV/0!` divide by zero, `#NAME?` mistyped name, `####` the column is too narrow.
if-and-or-iferror-logic: `=IF(test, if_true, if_false)` gives one of two results.
Text in a test goes in quotes: `=IF(B2="Paid", 0, D2)`.
`AND` is true only if all tests are true. `OR` is true if any is true. `NOT` reverses.
Nested `IF` handles more than two outcomes. Keep it to a few levels.
`=IFERROR(formula, "")` shows a tidy value instead of an error. Do not use it to hide real mistakes.
Common mistake: forgetting quotes around text, or a missing bracket.
sumif-countif-averageif-sumifs: `SUMIF(range, condition, sum_range)` adds only the rows that match.
Conditions with signs go in quotes: `">500"`, `"<>Paid"`.
Wildcards: `*` is any text, `?` is one character: `"A*"`.
`SUMIFS`, `COUNTIFS`, `AVERAGEIFS` use more than one condition. In `SUMIFS` the sum range comes first.
A total missing rows? Check for extra spaces or numbers stored as text.
vlookup-xlookup-index-match: `VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table, column_number, FALSE)` finds a value in the first column and returns another.
Always end with `FALSE` for an exact match.
`#N/A` means nothing was found. Check spaces, spelling and text versus number.
`VLOOKUP` cannot look left. `XLOOKUP` (365 and 2021) can, and it is simpler.
`INDEX` and `MATCH` work in every version: `MATCH` finds the position, `INDEX` returns the item.
Approximate match (`TRUE`) is for bands such as grades, and the table must be sorted.
text-functions-and-cleaning-data: `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `MID` take part of a text. `LEN` counts characters. `FIND` finds a position.
Text to Columns splits without formulas. Flash Fill copies a pattern you show it.
Remove Duplicates and Find and Replace clean quickly. `Ctrl+G`, Special, Blanks selects empty cells.
Golden rule: never clean your only copy. Keep the original on one sheet.
excel-dates-and-times: A date is a number: days counted from the start of 1900. Format it as a date.
`=TODAY()` is today's date. `=NOW()` includes the time. Both change when the file recalculates.
`EDATE` adds months. `EOMONTH` gives the end of the month.
`NETWORKDAYS` counts working days. Add a holiday list to skip them. `WORKDAY` finds a date.
`DATEDIF` gives age or length of service.
Problems: text dates, day and month swapped, a date that shows as a number.
sort-filter-and-excel-tables: Sort by one or more columns. Select the whole table so rows stay together.
Filter by text, number, date or colour. A filtered sheet hides rows, so say it when you share.
Excel Table (`Ctrl+T`): grows by itself, fills formulas, keeps headings visible, has a Total Row.
Good habits: one table per sheet, a heading in every column, no blank rows.
pivot-tables-for-beginners: A pivot table summarises a long table: totals by group, without formulas.
Four areas: Rows, Columns, Values, Filters.
Change Values from Sum to Count, Average, Min or Max.
Group dates by month or year. Add slicers to filter.
A pivot does not update by itself: right-click, Refresh.
A number looks wrong? Double-click it to see the rows behind it.
Source table: headings on row 1, no blanks, no merged cells.
excel-charts-and-simple-dashboard: Choose by question: columns or bars to compare, a line for change over time, a pie only for a few parts of a whole.
Write a clear title that says something, and label the axes with units.
Sort bars largest to smallest, and start bar charts at zero.
Use few colours: one for normal, one to highlight.
A simple dashboard: a few charts and key numbers on one sheet, from pivot tables.
Check the chart against the numbers. A wrong range can leave out the last row.
data-validation-conditional-formatting-p: Data validation lets only good entries in: whole number, list (drop-down), date, text length, custom.
A list that grows: base the drop-down on an Excel Table.
Conditional formatting colours cells by rule: highlight, top and bottom, data bars, colour scales, icons.
Formula rules colour the whole row: `=$D2>1000`.
Protect Sheet locks cells. It stops accidents, not determined people.
Before sharing: Check Accessibility and Inspect Document for hidden data.
print-share-and-keyboard-shortcuts: Print Area, Print Titles (repeat row 1 on every page), headers and footers with page numbers.
Page Break Preview shows where pages split. Save as PDF for a fixed layout.
Name files with a date or version. Check for hidden data before you send.
Treat salaries, phone numbers and ID numbers carefully. Share only with the right people.
Format Painter and templates save time.
excel-for-office-jobs-tests-and-next-ste: Employers usually test: formulas, `IF`, `VLOOKUP` or `XLOOKUP`, sorting and filtering, pivot tables, charts, formatting.
Practise real tasks: invoice, attendance sheet, expense tracker, stock register, marks sheet.
Describe your skills honestly. Say what you can do and what you are still learning.
In a test, read the question twice, check your totals, and keep the layout neat.
Next: `XLOOKUP`, `FILTER`, Power Query, Power Pivot, Google Sheets, then SQL or Python.
Spreadsheet mistakes are common. When numbers matter, check them twice.

workplace-english-tone-and-politeness: Clear beats fancy. Simple words and short sentences are professional.
Formal for people you do not know, customers and first emails. Neutral for most work messages. Informal for close colleagues.
Polite requests: `Could you...`, `Would you...`, `I would like...` (not `I want`).
Say the main thing first, then the details.
Soften a message: `Could you please...`, `I think...`, `It seems that...`.
Many kinds of English are correct: Indian, British, American and more. Be clear and respectful.
introduce-yourself-and-small-talk: Introduce yourself: `My name is...`, `I work in...`, `I am responsible for...`, `I joined last month.`
Introduce another person: say their name and role, and why they should meet.
Safe small talk: the day, the journey, the weather, food and breaks, the weekend.
Be careful with money, age, religion, politics and personal life.
Keep it going: ask an open question and listen. End politely: `It was nice talking to you.`
Did not understand? `Sorry, could you say that again?`
clear-sentences-and-common-english-mista: Present simple for habits, present continuous for now: `I work here`, `I am working on a report`.
Subject and verb must agree: `He works`, `They work`.
Articles: `a` and `an` for one of many, `the` for a specific one.
Some nouns have no plural: `information`, `advice`. Say `a piece of advice`.
Since a point in time, for a length of time. Fewer for things you count, less for things you cannot.
Fix the two or three mistakes you make most. Check for them before you send.
email-structure-subject-greeting-closing: Five parts: subject line, greeting, opening line, body, closing and signature.
The subject says what the email is about. Be specific: `Invoice 1042: payment date`.
Opening line: why you are writing, in one sentence.
Body: short paragraphs or a list. State what you need and by when.
Reply answers the sender. Reply All answers everyone, so use it only when needed. CC is for information.
Check before you send: right person, attachment, spelling, tone. Write nothing you would not want others to read.
requests-replies-and-follow-up-emails: Ask: `Could you please send...`, `I would be grateful if...`. Say what and by when.
Reply: answer the question first, then add details.
Sending an attachment: `Please find attached...`. Check that it is attached.
Follow up politely after a few days: `I am following up on my email of...`.
Connecting words: first, then, because, so, however, also, for example.
apologies-complaints-and-saying-no-polit: Apologise: say sorry, say what went wrong, say what you will do to fix it.
Complaint: stay calm, give facts, say what you need.
Say no politely: thank, give a short reason, offer an alternative.
Bad news: say it early and clearly, then say what happens next.
Disagree politely: `I see your point, but...`.
Angry message? Wait before you answer. Nobody has to accept harassment or threats at work.
chat-messages-teams-whatsapp-etiquette: Chat for quick questions. Email for formal or longer messages. Call when it is complicated or urgent.
A clear chat message: greeting, the question, and what you need.
One message with the full point is better than many small ones.
Tone is easy to misread in chat. Be polite and short.
Group chats: check who is in the group. No private or critical messages about a person.
Respect time, do not message late at night, and never share passwords or customer data.
reports-notes-and-meeting-minutes: Plain English: short sentences (15 to 20 words), simple words, active voice, be specific.
Put the conclusion first and the details after. Use headings and lists.
Incident report: when and where, who, what happened (facts only), action taken, what happens next.
Short report: title and date, summary, background, findings, recommendation.
Minutes: date, who was there, decisions, actions with names and dates.
Write only what you know. Do not guess or blame.
phone-calls-and-voicemail-english: Answer: `Good morning, [company], [name] speaking. How can I help you?`
Make a call: say who you are, why you call, and who you want.
Ask to repeat or slow down: `Could you say that again, please?`
Spell names and emails slowly, with clear examples for letters.
Take a message: name, number, reason. Read it back to check.
Voicemail: name, number, short reason, when you can be reached. Never say yes when you did not understand.
speak-up-in-meetings: Prepare: read the agenda, one or two points, one question, your numbers.
Opinion: `I think...`, `In my view...`. Agree: `I agree with...`.
Disagree politely: `I see it differently because...`.
Interrupt politely: `Sorry to interrupt, may I add something?`
Did not catch it: `Could you repeat that, please?`
Make your first contribution early, even a small question. Summarise and confirm actions at the end.
understand-accents-and-listen-better: Speech is hard because words run together, stress and rhythm change, accents differ, and speakers are fast.
Listen for key words: numbers, names, dates, verbs, nouns. You do not need every word.
Use the context and do not stop at one unknown word.
Check what you heard: say it back in your own words.
Daily routine: listen once for the idea, listen again in short pieces, read the transcript, repeat aloud.
Keep a small list of new words and phrases.
presentations-and-explaining-your-work: Start with the audience and one message. What should they remember? What should they do?
Simple structure: opening, main points, summary.
Slides: one idea each, few words, pictures and charts, do not read the slide.
Explain a chart: what it shows, the main point, what it means.
Nerves: practise aloud, learn the first 30 seconds, breathe, speak slowly.
For questions: listen, repeat the question, answer, or say you will find out.
customer-service-english: LEAP: Listen, Empathise, Act, follow up (Perform).
Greet warmly and find out what the customer needs. Ask open questions.
Empathy: `I understand`, `I am sorry about that`.
Cannot say yes? Explain why and offer what you can do.
Angry customer: stay calm, let them speak, apologise, ask for facts, say what you will do and when.
Do not promise what you cannot do. If someone is abusive or threatens you, follow your company rules.
feedback-teamwork-and-your-manager: Receiving feedback: listen, say thank you, ask questions, do not argue.
Giving feedback: be specific, talk about the work and not the person, suggest a next step.
Ask for help early and say what you already tried.
Report a problem or delay early. Hiding it makes it worse.
Say no or set limits politely: `I cannot take this on today, but I can do it on Thursday.`
Multicultural team: speak simply, check understanding, be patient, be careful with jokes.
improve-your-english-every-day-plan: Start with your goal and a small 30-day target.
Daily routine: listening, reading, writing, speaking. A little every day beats a lot once a week.
Keep a personal phrase book of useful phrases you hear and use.
Use English at work: one real email or comment a week.
Measure progress: record yourself and compare after a month.
30 days: Week 1 goal and routine, Week 2 real use, Week 3 speaking partner, Week 4 review.

how-fresher-interviews-work: Usual stages: application, screening call, written or online test, interview rounds, offer and checks.
Screening checks you are reachable and clear. The test checks accuracy under time. The technical round checks basics. The managerial and HR rounds check fit and expectations.
Practice differs by country and company. Campus drives, group discussions and competency questions are common in different places.
Formats: one to one, panel, group discussion, phone or video, walk-in.
An interview is two-way. You are allowed to ask questions too.
Make a first checklist: documents, route, time, prep sheet.
research-the-company-and-role: Start with the job advert: list the skills and tasks they ask for.
Do not claim skills you do not have. `I have not used that tool yet, but I have used...` is fine.
Learn about the company: website, About page, social page, recent news, careful use of reviews.
Understand the role in daily terms: what will you do on a normal day?
Prepare your own questions to ask them.
Write a one-page prep sheet with five lines about the company.
know-your-resume-and-projects: Only write what you can explain. Exaggerated claims are easy to test.
Each project in three parts: the problem, your part (say `I`), the result and what you learned.
Be ready to talk about internships, part-time jobs and volunteering.
Prove each skill with a small example.
Check the facts on the page: dates, marks, names.
tell-me-about-yourself-answer: Present: who you are and what you do now. Past: two or three relevant things. Future: why this job.
Include facts that match the job. Leave out your life story, age, family and negative comments.
Career gap or change: say it briefly, say what you did or learned, then move on.
Nervous? Breathe and start slowly. In an online interview, look at the camera.
strengths-and-weaknesses-answers: Strength: say it, then prove it with a short real example.
Fresher strengths: learning fast, reliability, teamwork, communication, attention to detail, problem solving, responsibility.
Weakness: be honest, pick a safe one, and say what you are doing about it.
Avoid `I am a perfectionist`, a weakness that hurts the role, blaming others, or `I have none`.
Related: biggest achievement, how friends describe you, what you do when you do not know something.
Not sure what to say? Ask a friend or teacher when they saw you do well.
why-this-company-why-hire-you: Why here? Use honest reasons: the work, what you can learn, the product or mission, practical fit, growth.
Why hire you? Formula: Need, Match, Proof, Close.
Name what the job needs, two things you have, one real example, and how it helps the team.
`What do you know about our company?` Use your research lines.
Five years: show ambition that fits the role.
If you know little about the company, say so honestly and show interest.
behavioural-questions-star-method: Action is the longest part. Say `I` and what you personally did.
End with the result and what you learned.
Common questions: teamwork, a difficult customer, a deadline, a mistake.
Build a story bank of 5 to 6 real stories you can adapt.
Mistake stories are fine: show what you learned and changed.
no-experience-gaps-career-change-questio: Calm formula: acknowledge, give a short honest reason, show what you did meanwhile, return to the present and the job.
No experience: talk about projects, practice, learning and the skills you bring.
Employment gap: say it briefly and say what you did or learned.
Career change: connect your earlier skills to the new role.
Low marks: be honest, show how you improved.
Do not know the answer? Say so, then explain how you would find out.
aptitude-and-written-tests: Tests may cover numbers, verbal ability, logical reasoning, subject questions, situational judgement, typing and practical skills.
Know the format first: time, number of questions, negative marking.
Four weeks: basics, topic practice, speed, full mock tests.
Keep an error log. Read the question twice. Skip and come back.
Practise mental maths and read English daily.
Not passed? You will know the format next time.
technical-round-preparation: Interviewers look for strong basics, your own work, clear thinking, honesty and willingness to learn.
Depth beats breadth: know eight topics well.
Explain your projects: the problem, your part, what you would improve.
Think aloud: repeat the problem, give an example, start simple, work step by step, check edge cases.
Do not know? Say so, then reason it out. Do not guess wildly.
Ask a good question at the end.
group-discussion-and-case-questions: Observers watch content, communication, listening, teamwork and behaviour.
Think for a moment before you speak. A short, clear first point is good.
Add one new point each time, use real examples, include quiet people, summarise near the end.
Disagree politely: `I see your point, but I see it differently because...`.
Case questions: clarify, structure, explore, conclude.
Quality beats quantity. Two or three strong points are enough.
phone-and-video-interviews: Test technology a day before: internet, software, charger, audio, camera.
Quiet room, plain background, light on your face, notifications off.
Phone: sit or stand upright, smile, speak a little slower, take notes.
Video: join 5 to 10 minutes early, look at the camera, no script, no other screens.
Something goes wrong? Rejoin quickly or call the recruiter. Say sorry briefly and carry on.
Practise once with a friend on the same platform.
salary-notice-period-and-your-questions: Research the salary range for similar roles before the interview.
You can ask for their range first. If asked, give a range, not one number.
Notice period and joining date: be honest and clear.
Ask about hours, shifts, probation, bonds and documents.
A real employer does not charge you money for a job.
`Do you have any questions for us?` Always ask one or two. Avoid asking only about pay and leave.
interview-day-checklist-and-job-scams: Day before: confirm details, plan the journey, prepare clothes and bag, sleep.
Carry documents, copies of your resume, a pen, a notebook and water.
Arrive early, be polite to everyone, and switch the phone to silent.
Scam signs: they ask for money, offer a job with no real interview, pay is too good, personal email addresses, early requests for bank or OTP details, pressure.
Check the company: website, address, phone, reviews. Do not pay fees.
Paid or shared something? Contact your bank at once and change passwords.
after-the-interview-follow-up-and-reject: Write notes the same day: questions, what went well, what to improve.
Send a short thank-you message within 24 hours.
Wait for the time they told you. Then follow up politely once.
Offer: thank them and take time to check the details.
Rejection: reply politely, ask for feedback once, choose one or two things to improve.
Keep a simple job search tracker. Look after yourself, then restart.

your-phone-is-your-job-tool: A phone number that works, and a voicemail or message that sounds professional.
A simple email address with your name.
Never give your email password, bank PIN or OTP to anyone.
Make space on your phone and keep a folder for your job papers.
Save data and battery. Keep the phone safe with a screen lock.
Check that calls from employers reach you.
know-your-skills-and-write-them-down: Write what you do in small tasks, not only the job title.
Write your tools and machines, your years and places, training and papers.
Write your good habits: on time, careful, safe.
Make a simple skills sheet. You will use it for your resume and interviews.
Do not write a skill you do not have. You can lose the job.
Little formal work? Count training, family business, practice and volunteering.
make-a-one-page-resume-on-your-phone: One page, plain layout, true facts, newest work first, clear contact details.
Order: name and contact, short summary, skills, work history, training and licences, languages.
Summary: two lines. Who you are, what work you do, how long.
Make it on your phone and save it as a PDF.
Ask a friend to read it for mistakes.
No resume yet? Start with the skills sheet and a short message.
photos-of-your-papers-and-privacy: Take a clear photo in good light, flat, with all four corners visible.
Make the file small and name it clearly.
Safe to send early: resume, trade certificate, safety training, reference letter.
Send later, after a real offer and checks: copy of ID, bank details.
Never send your ATM card, PIN, OTP or online banking password.
Cover what is not needed. Keep the originals safe.
where-to-look-for-work: Job sites and apps, people you know, local contractors, shops and factories.
Training centres, government help, agencies, and groups on WhatsApp, Facebook or Telegram.
Use many ways at once. Many people need weeks or months, so be patient.
Keep a simple list: where you applied, date, answer.
Tell people what work you want.
apply-by-phone-messages-and-follow-up: A short message: your name, the job, two facts about you, and your phone number.
An email needs a clear subject line: `Application for electrician job - Sunil Kumar`.
Phone call: prepare, call mid-morning, say who you are, ask a clear question, write down details, say thank you.
Do not understand? `Sorry, can you say that again, please?`
Follow up politely after a few days.
Keep a record and answer employer calls clearly.
spot-job-scams-and-stay-safe: Warning signs: they ask for money, the pay is too good, they want ID or bank details early, they hurry you.
No real address or company name, offers from strangers, chat only, bad writing and strange links are also signs.
Check before you trust: search the company, call the official number, ask for the offer in writing, visit by day, ask someone you trust.
Slow down. A real job will still be there tomorrow.
Tricked? Do not feel ashamed. Tell your bank, change passwords and report it.
Work in another country needs extra care. Check the agent and the papers.
prepare-for-the-interview-and-trade-test: Before the day: confirm, plan the way, prepare clothes and papers, rest, practise answers.
Bring copies of your resume, certificates, licences and ID.
On the day: arrive early, greet everyone politely, switch the phone to silent.
Answer simply and honestly. Know your safety rules.
Practical test: work carefully and safely, and say what you are doing.
Ask about the work, hours, safety and pay. Say thank you after.
know-your-rights-pay-and-written-agreeme: Ask for the offer in writing: company, job, pay, hours, start date.
If you cannot read it well, ask a trusted person before you sign.
Know the pay, how and when it is paid, and about overtime.
Know the hours and rest times, and the safety rules.
Keep proof: messages, agreements, pay slips, photos of notices.
Something wrong? Ask politely first, then use the local help office. Rules differ by country.
keep-learning-and-your-seven-day-plan: Day 1 phone, Day 2 skills sheet, Day 3 resume, Day 4 paper photos.
Day 5 look for jobs and tell five people, Day 6 apply three times, Day 7 follow up and check for scams.
Keep your energy up: rest, eat, talk to people.
Learn one new thing at a time. Use free phone videos.
See where your skills can go: a higher trade, a supervisor, your own work.
This course cannot promise a job. It gives practical steps.
